blocks.text: 如今，代理和机器人能做什么与互联网其余部分允许它们做什么之间的斗争已经持续了一段时间，但最近的升级确实似乎体现在数据中：

inlines.text: 如今，代理和机器人能做什么与互联网其余部分允许它们做什么之间的斗争已经持续了一段时间，但最近的升级确实似乎体现在数据中：

blocks.text: 根据 Cloudflare 的数据，自夏季以来，代理和机器人收到的 403“Forbidden”响应占比大幅上升（约为过去的两倍）。

inlines.text: 根据 Cloudflare 的数据，自夏季以来，代理和机器人收到的 403“Forbidden”响应占比大幅上升（约为过去的两倍）。

blocks.text: 这是否是专门针对“代理式商务”的回应是另一个问题，但想必这至少是部分原因。电商不想被去中介化是可以理解的，它们不仅会失去客户关系，还会失去那些为大型电商平台带来可观广告收入的客户眼球。

blocks.text: 除了平台优势被侵蚀之外，Amazon 们对代理式商务感到担忧可能还有其他原因。这些其他担忧中首当其冲的可能是欺诈和退货，这两者对整个电商而言都是日益严重的祸患：

inlines.text: 除了平台优势被侵蚀之外，Amazon 们对代理式商务感到担忧可能还有其他原因。这些其他担忧中首当其冲的可能是欺诈和退货，这两者对整个电商而言都是日益严重的祸患：

blocks.text: 根据 NRF 的数据，自 2019 年以来，退货率和退货总成本分别基本翻了一番和增至三倍。同样，报告的欺诈行为普遍存在，最常见的担忧是“争议滥用”，即客户购买了某物后又对扣款提出争议。如果发卡机构站在客户一边，商家就只能自认倒霉。

blocks.text: 不难理解为什么电商会担心代理式商务可能让本已恶化的问题雪上加霜。“哦，我的代理买了那件用亮片拼出我名字的个性化校队夹克，不是我买的，我绝不会那样做”，或者“我告诉我的代理以最优价格买袜子，但我没想到它会找到‘10,000 双菱形花纹袜，批发特价’，所以请寄来退货标签和一辆叉车。”

blocks.text: 然而，还有另一个问题可能正在阻碍机器人购物狂潮：消费者可能实际上（还）并不想要他们的机器人替他们购物。

inlines.text: 然而，还有另一个问题可能正在阻碍机器人购物狂潮：消费者可能实际上（还）并不

blocks.text: 截至目前（至少根据某些数据），消费者似乎普遍愿意接受 AI 帮助他们找到想要的东西，尤其是帮助他们找到最优价格，但在实际完成购买时，消费者似乎有些抗拒：

blocks.text: 约 25% 的受访者表示，他们愿意让 AI 为他们购买各种消费品（奢侈品除外），但 42% 的人表示他们完全不相信 AI 能代表他们进行购买。这不到一半，但仍比人们预期的要多。

blocks.text: 看来，就目前而言，消费者——和电商一样——也担心误购、烦人的退货和拒付争议。此外，可能人们就是喜欢自己购物，至少在最终购买决定上是这样。

blocks.text: 顺着这个思路，来自 Similarweb 的一些点击流数据（虽然有点过时）似乎印证了这一点：AI 适合用来咨询，但购买（目前）仍是人类的事。似乎有越来越多的“购物旅程”会在进入实际结账页面之前先访问 AI，但实际上绝大多数 AI 购物会话似乎都处于旅程的“中间阶段”，也就是在发现与购买之间：

blocks.text: 除了惊叹于（超级）帕累托分布的顽固之外，实在很难说这到底意味着什么，但 Charts 还是试着解读一下。

一方面，制作大量大量视频似乎是推动销售的好方法，这意味着购物体验中显然有某种“个人化”的东西是代理难以复制的（不过，如果 Muse 直播它的旅程，情况或许会改变）。
另一方面，如果代理式商务真的起飞，那么对于这一小群但极具影响力的高产内容创作者来说意味着什么？他们通过一种与代理毫无关联的媒介来推动销售。

blocks.text: 当然，代理式商务和社交电商不必互相排斥。零售业规模巨大，容得下不止一种模式。但总体来看，我们如今的购物方式在某种程度上是为人类界面而优化的，以至于“只要加上代理”可能低估了这一点。

blocks.text: 高价的解药就是高价

inlines.text: 高价的解药就是高价

blocks.text: Charts 无意在“通胀：会还是不会”的争论中站队，但它愿意花点时间思考那句老话——“高价的解药就是高价”，因为这确实值得一番考量。

inlines.text: Charts 无意在“通胀：会还是不会”的争论中站队，但它愿意花点时间思考那句老话——“高价的解药就是高价”，因为这确实值得一番考量。

blocks.text: 基本前提很简单：如果价格涨得足够高，就会抑制需求——要么是对该商品本身的需求，要么是对其他商品的需求，因为需求方为这个如今更贵的东西花了太多钱，就再也负担不起其他东西了。众所周知，当需求下降时，价格往往会随之下降……所以，如果高价最终抑制了需求，而受抑制的需求又导致价格下跌，那么高价的解药就是……高价。

blocks.text: Whether that’s a response specifically to “agentic commerce” is a separate question, but presumably that’s at least some part of what’s going on. Etailers understandably don’t want to be disintermediated, and not only lose their customer relationships, but also lose those customer eyeballs that are a substantial source of advertising revenue for the large ecomm platforms.

Likewise, reported fraud is pervasive, with the most common concern being “dispute abuse,” i.e. customers buying something and then later disputing the charge. On the one hand, it seems that making a lot a lot of videos is a good way to drive sales, which implies there’s something evidently “personal” about the shopping experience that would be hard for an agent to replicate (although perhaps if Muse live-streamed its journey, that could change).

On the other hand, if agentic commerce really does take off, then what would it mean for this small, but mighty cohort of prolific content creators who drive sales through a medium that has no relevance to an agent whatsoever?

blocks.text: Of course, agentic commerce and social commerce do not have to be mutually exclusive. Retail is really big, and there’s plenty of room for more than one model. But, it does seem broadly true that the way we shop now is optimized for a human interface to a degree that “just add agents” may be underestimating.

blocks.text: Cure To High Prices Is High Prices

inlines.text: Cure To High Prices Is High Prices

blocks.text: Charts has no intention of weighing in one way or another on the “inflation: will it, won’t it” debate, but it will take a moment to reflect on the old saying that “the cure to high prices is high prices,” because it certainly seems worthy of some consideration.

inlines.text: Charts has no intention of weighing in one way or another on the “inflation: will it, won’t it” debate, but it will take a moment to reflect on the old saying that “the cure to high prices is high prices,” because it certainly seems worthy of some consideration.

blocks.text: The basic premise is straightforward: if prices get high enough, they suppress demand—either for that thing, or some other thing(s) that demand can no longer afford because demand is paying so much for the now more expensive thing. As everyone knows, when demand falls, prices tend to follow . . . so if high prices eventually suppress demand, and suppressed demand leads to falling prices, then the cure to high prices is . . . high prices.

blocks.text: But that doesn’t mean high prices are having no effect on demand. Hyperscalers may still be on a chip-buying spree, but everyone else appears to be saving their hardware upgrades for another day:

blocks.text: Just taking PCs as an example, according to IDC, PC shipments have dropped substantially since the beginning of the year.

blocks.text: It’s not just PCs that are facing some demand headwinds, but iPhones, as well, all of which have gotten more expensive, partly as a result of the AI buildout. Now, is it definitely the case that high prices are the reason that fewer PCs and iPhones are shipping? No, but it seems like a pretty good guess. And if that’s true, then the old adage appears to be working its way through the system (and will perhaps be reflected in softer prices, soon enough).

blocks.text: According to some data and analysis from PNC Bank, Zoomers are actually doing pretty well, from a financial standpoint. Not only are they doing well, but Gen Z is doing considerably better in 2025 than Millennials were doing 10 years ago (when Millennials were Zoomer-aged):

inlines.text: According to some data and analysis from PNC Bank, Zoomers are actually doing pretty well, from a financial standpoint. Not only are they doing well, but Gen Z is doing considerably better in 2025 than Millennials were doing 10 years ago (when Millennials were Zoomer-aged):

blocks.text: Zoomers enjoy real incomes that are 20-40% higher than what their Millennial elders suffered at every part of the income distribution. Point-in-time generational comps are imperfect, but it’s still not the result most would expect to find.

blocks.text: It’s also not just higher incomes where Zoomers are winning. There’s also data that suggests Zoomers face lower unemployment, have higher net worths, more liquid assets, and bigger retirement accounts, then the previous generation did at an equivalent stage of life.

blocks.text: According to PNC’s internal data, Zoomers spend more of their income than Millennials and leave less in the rainy-day fund, as well.

blocks.text: In terms of what Zoomers are spending their money on, they allocate more to retirement, shelter, and transportation, and substantially less to education and energy:

blocks.text: At the category level, Zoomers also allocate relatively more to gambling and devices, but relatively less to clothing and sustenance.

blocks.text: Save more for retirement (but keep less in the rainy-day fund), while also hitting the tables and the money line, but sparing the booze. It’s an odd combination, but it’s Zoomer money, and they can spend it how they please.

blocks.text: Well, perhaps, “please” is the wrong word, because whatever their material advantages over generations prior, the Zoomer mood is decidedly dour:

blocks.text: Since 2017 (with a partial reprieve during pandemania), the traditional “sentiment” advantage that 18-34 year-olds typically enjoy relative to the broader population has all but evaporated. The Zoomers are not as cheerful as young folks of yore.

blocks.text: Now, consumer confidence is a very noisy series that has lost even more signal since the pandemic, likely because of falling response rates (among other things), but even if it’s noisier, it’s strange (but possible) that the noise would be isolated to 18-34 year-olds. In other words, even if the headline “confidence” figure is less reliable, one would think the ratios within ought to stay relatively stable . . . and in this case, it appears they haven’t: Zoomers are no more confident than anyone else, which makes them unlike all the young people of generations prior (at least through the ‘70s).

blocks.text: Taking this at face value, it would appear that the data does validate the vibe . . . but however bad the vibes may be, it’s hard to blame finances. That doesn’t mean Zoomers are without other reasons to feel relatively less optimistic, but certainly when it comes to making and spending money, they seem to be doing just fine.
